mainEntity.name: How painful is dental implant recovery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most patients describe the discomfort following dental implant placement as manageable and comparable to that of a tooth extraction. The peak period of soreness typically occurs within the first two to three days and responds well to over-the-counter pain relief as recommended by your dental team. By the end of the first week, discomfort has usually reduced significantly. Every patient's pain threshold and experience is different, and your dental team will provide personalised aftercare guidance tailored to your procedure and needs.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally after a dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the immediate days following surgery, a soft food diet is advised to avoid disturbing the surgical site. Foods such as soup, yoghurt, mashed potato, and scrambled eggs are generally well tolerated. As healing progresses over the following weeks, most patients can gradually return to a broader diet. Your dental team will advise you on when it is appropriate to resume chewing on the implant side, and this should not be rushed until the restoration is in place and integration has been confirmed.

mainEntity.name: What is peri-implantitis and how can I avoid it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the gum and bone tissue surrounding a dental implant, and it is considered one of the more significant long-term risk factors for implant failure. It is broadly analogous to periodontitis (gum disease) affecting natural teeth. Risk factors include poor oral hygiene, smoking, and a history of gum disease. It can be largely prevented through diligent daily cleaning around the implant, regular professional hygiene appointments, and avoiding smoking. Early detection at routine check-ups allows for timely management.

mainEntity.name: Does dental implant healing differ depending on where the implant is placed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the location of the implant within the mouth can influence healing to some degree. Implants placed in the upper jaw (maxilla) may take slightly longer to fully integrate than those placed in the lower jaw (mandible), partly due to differences in bone density between the two arches. Implants in the back of the mouth (posterior region) may also face different healing considerations compared with those placed at the front. Your dental clinician will account for the specific placement site when discussing your individual treatment timeline.

mainEntity.name: What happens if a dental implant fails to integrate?

acceptedAnswer.text: In a small proportion of cases, osseointegration does not proceed as expected and the implant may fail to achieve the necessary stability. Signs of this can include pain, mobility of the implant, or radiographic evidence of bone loss. In such circumstances, the implant is typically removed and the site is given time to heal before any decision is made about whether a further attempt may be clinically appropriate. Implant failure does not always preclude re-treatment, but this would need to be assessed individually by a qualified clinician.

mainEntity.name: Is there anything that can speed up dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: While there is no proven method to dramatically accelerate osseointegration, supporting your body's natural healing processes is worthwhile. Maintaining good nutritional intake — particularly adequate vitamin D, calcium, and protein — supports bone and tissue repair. Avoiding smoking, following your dental team's hygiene instructions carefully, and attending all scheduled appointments can help create a favourable healing environment. Some clinics may discuss the role of supplementary protocols, but patients should treat any claims about accelerated healing with appropriate scepticism and discuss these with their clinical team.
